title: Object-oriented programming
summary: Bundle data and behaviour together using classes and objects, so your code models real things and stays organised as it grows.
objectives: Explain what a class and an object are, and how they relate
Define a class with the class keyword and create instances
Use __init__ to set up an object's attributes
Write methods that act on an object's own data via self
Distinguish instance attributes from class attributes
Understand inheritance to reuse and extend a class
Recognise when objects make code clearer than loose functions

quiz.q: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint; an object is a built instance of it
An object is a blueprint; a class is built from it
A class is a function and an object is its return value
quiz.why: A class describes what objects of that type look like and do; each object is a concrete instance created from that blueprint.

options: Runs automatically when an object is created to set up its attributes
quiz.why: __init__ is the constructor — Python calls it automatically when you create an instance, so you can set the object's starting attributes.

quiz.q: What does the self parameter refer to inside a method?
quiz.answer: The particular object the method is being called on, so the method can read and change that object's own attributes.
quiz.why: Each method receives self as its first parameter; it lets the method work with the specific instance's data.

quiz.q: Which line correctly creates an object from a class named Dog?
quiz.why: In Python you call the class like a function — Dog() — which builds and returns a new instance.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is inheritance?
quiz.answer: A way to build a new class on top of an existing one so it reuses that class's attributes and methods and can add or override its own.
quiz.why: Inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent's code and specialise it, avoiding duplication.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
options: A class attribute is shared by all instances; an instance attribute belongs to one object
A class attribute belongs to one object; an instance attribute is shared
quiz.why: Class attributes are defined on the class and shared; instance attributes are set per object, usually in __init__ via self.

body_markdown:
## Why objects?

So far you've kept **data** in variables and **behaviour** in functions, separately. Object-oriented programming, or OOP, lets you bundle related data and the functions that act on it into one thing called an **object**.

Think of a bank account: it has data (a balance, an owner) and behaviour (deposit, withdraw). Keeping these together in one object is cleaner than passing a loose balance variable around between functions.

## Classes vs objects

A **class** is a blueprint. An **object** (also called an *instance*) is a concrete thing built from that blueprint. One class, many objects — just like one cookie cutter makes many cookies.

```python
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()      # an object
bella = Dog()    # another object
```

## The __init__ method and self

`__init__` runs automatically when you create an object. It sets up the object's starting **attributes**. The first parameter, `self`, refers to the specific object being built.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.name)   # Rex
```

## Methods

A **method** is a function defined inside a class. It always takes `self` first, so it can use the object's own data.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def bark(self):
        return self.name + " says woof!"

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(rex.bark())   # Rex says woof!
```

## Inheritance

**Inheritance** lets a new class build on an existing one, reusing its code and adding or changing behaviour. The new class is the *child*; the original is the *parent*.

```python
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def speak(self):
        return "..."

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return self.name + " says meow"

print(Cat("Bella").speak())   # Bella says meow
```

## Your task

Write a `BankAccount` class with a balance, plus `deposit` and `withdraw` methods that update it.

slides.title: Object-oriented programming
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we'll explore object-oriented programming, often shortened to O O P. It's a way of organising your code around objects that bundle data and behaviour together. By the end you'll be able to write your own classes, create objects from them, give them methods, and even share code between classes using inheritance. This is a foundational idea you'll meet everywhere in real Python projects.

slides.title: Why objects?
bullets: Bundle related data and behaviour together.
One object instead of loose variables and functions.
Models real things: an account, a user, a model.
Keeps code organised as it grows.
slides.narration: So far you've kept data in variables and behaviour in functions, completely separate. Object-oriented programming lets you bundle them together into a single thing called an object. Picture a bank account. It has data, like a balance and an owner, and behaviour, like deposit and withdraw. Wrapping those together in one object is far cleaner than passing a loose balance variable around between functions.

slides.title: Classes vs objects
bullets: A class is a blueprint.
An object is an instance built from it.
One class can make many objects.
Like a cookie cutter making many cookies.
slides.code:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
bella = Dog()
slides.narration: Two words you'll hear constantly: class and object. A class is a blueprint that describes what something looks like and what it can do. An object, also called an instance, is a concrete thing built from that blueprint. One class can produce many objects, just like one cookie cutter stamps out many cookies. Here, Dog is the class, and rex and bella are two separate objects.

slides.title: Setting up with __init__
bullets: __init__ runs when you create an object.
It sets the object's starting attributes.
self refers to the object being built.
Attributes are data attached to the object.
slides.narration: To give an object its starting data, we use a special method called dunder init, written with two underscores on each side. Python runs it automatically the moment you create an object. The first parameter, self, refers to the specific object being built. So when we write self dot name equals name, we're attaching a name attribute to this particular dog. Creating Dog with Rex and three sets those values.

slides.title: Reading attributes
bullets: Access attributes with dot notation.
Each object keeps its own values.
rex.name and bella.name are independent.
slides.code:
rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
bella = Dog("Bella", 5)

print(rex.name)     # Rex
print(bella.age)    # 5
slides.narration: Once an object has attributes, you read them using dot notation: the object's name, a dot, then the attribute. Crucially, each object keeps its own separate copy of the data. Rex dot name gives Rex, while bella dot name gives Bella. They were built from the same class, but they're completely independent objects with their own values.

slides.title: Methods: behaviour on objects
bullets: A method is a function inside a class.
It always takes self first.
self lets it use the object's own data.
Call it with object.method().
slides.narration: Objects don't just hold data, they do things. A method is a function defined inside a class. Every method takes self as its first parameter, which gives it access to the object's own data. Here, bark uses self dot name to build its message. You call a method with the object, a dot, and the method name, like rex dot bark. Notice you don't pass self yourself; Python fills it in for you.

slides.title: Class vs instance attributes
bullets: Instance attributes belong to one object.
Class attributes are shared by all objects.
Define class attributes in the class body.
Define instance attributes in __init__.
slides.narration: There are two kinds of attributes. Instance attributes, set with self inside dunder init, belong to one object only. Class attributes are written directly in the class body and are shared by every object of that class. In this example, every dog shares the same species, Canis, but each has its own name. Use class attributes for things that are genuinely the same across all instances.

slides.title: Inheritance
bullets: Build a new class on an existing one.
The child reuses the parent's code.
It can add or override methods.
Avoids copying the same code twice.
slides.narration: Inheritance lets you build a new class on top of an existing one. The new class, the child, automatically reuses everything from the parent class, and can add new methods or override existing ones. Here, Cat inherits from Animal but replaces speak with its own version. Inheritance saves you from copying the same code into many classes, and you'll see it constantly in libraries you'll use later in this course.

slides.title: Why it matters for A I
bullets: Libraries model things as classes.
A model, a dataset, a layer are objects.
You'll create and configure them constantly.
OOP makes large codebases manageable.
slides.narration: Why care about this for an A I career? Because the libraries you'll work with are built entirely from classes. A machine learning model, a dataset, a neural network layer, each is an object you create and configure. Understanding classes, objects, and methods means you'll read and use these tools with confidence rather than copying code you don't understand. O O P is the language that large, real-world codebases are written in.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting self as the first parameter.
Forgetting self when setting attributes.
Confusing the class with an object of it.
Calling a method without parentheses.
slides.narration: Let's flag the slip-ups beginners make. One: forgetting self as the first parameter of a method. Two: writing name equals name instead of self dot name, so the value never sticks to the object. Three: confusing the class itself with an object built from it. And four: writing rex dot bark without parentheses, which refers to the method instead of calling it. Watch for these four and you'll avoid most early confusion.

bullets: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance.
__init__ and self set up an object's attributes.
Methods give objects behaviour.
Inheritance reuses and extends a class.
Task: write a BankAccount class with deposit & withdraw.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A class is a blueprint, and an object is a concrete instance built from it. Dunder init, together with self, sets up each object's attributes. Methods give your objects behaviour, and inheritance lets one class reuse and extend another. Your task before the next lesson: write a bank account class with a balance, plus deposit and withdraw methods that update it. Build it, test it, and you'll have truly understood objects. See you next time.
